title: China seizes PCTC orders as Europe pivots, South Korea targets LNG carriers
summary: China's surging automobile exports have triggered a massive PCTC ordering spree, with Chinese shipyards securing 56 of 58 global orders this year. This rapid fleet expansion, alarmingly including the high-value trade of a 26-year-old PCTC, prioritizes immediate capacity over crucial decarbonisation efforts. Without immediate and stringent adoption of low-carbon fuels and technologies, this surge guarantees a substantial rise in maritime emissions and future FuelEU Maritime compliance headaches.
content:
China’s solo dominance is hardening in the global pure car and truck carrier (PCTC) ordering market. As China’s automobile export volumes surge and Chinese shipbuilders absorb the carrier demand, European shipping companies that had assigned work to Korea and others are also said to have recently placed large-scale orders in China.

According to Clarksons Research, a British shipbuilding and shipping market analysis firm, 58 new PCTCs were ordered worldwide from the start of the year through last month. China won orders for 56 of them.

In 2023 and 2024, PCTC orders were 83 and 73 ships, respectively, but amid concerns about oversupply last year, orders plunged to nine. However, this year, as China’s automobile exports increased, projections grew that there were not enough ships to transport them, expanding PCTC demand again.

According to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM), in the first half of this year China exported 5,096,000 vehicles, up 65.3% from the same period a year earlier. In June alone, auto exports reached 1,037,000, surpassing 1 million for the first time.

While China’s automobile export volumes have surged, PCTC supply is short, and demand for secondhand vessels has also increased sharply. In July, a 26-year-old 4,310 CEU-class PCTC in China sold for about $42 million, three times the minimum bid price of about $14 million. One CEU is space for one car, and the ship was a mid-sized PCTC capable of carrying about 4,300 passenger cars.

China’s auto industry has remarked on a shortage of carriers. According to Reuters and other foreign media, executives at Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD said on this month’s first-half earnings conference call that “overseas exports were hampered by transport constraints this year,” adding, “if transport had been smooth, exports would have been higher.”

As PCTC demand rose, Chinese automakers and shipping companies signed construction contracts with domestic shipyards to secure their fleets. According to Greek maritime outlet Loban Asaphina, BYD this month ordered 10 9,200 CEU-class PCTCs from a Chinese shipyard. China-registered Hong Kong carrier Zhongnan Shipping is also said to have ordered four PCTCs in July from Jiangsu New Yangzi Shipbuilding in Jiangsu province.

Overseas carriers are also expanding their fleets. This year, European carriers have signed 33 construction contracts with Chinese shipyards. The company that ordered the most ships among them is Italy’s Grimaldi, which ordered a total of 12 PCTCs from three Chinese shipbuilders.

The concentration of PCTC orders from Chinese and overseas carriers at Chinese shipbuilders is not just due to strong price competitiveness. Because PCTCs do not require cutting-edge technology, construction demand flows to places that can build at lower unit costs. The fact that Korean shipyards’ docks are saturated with large container ships and liquefied natural gas carriers (LNGCs) is also cited as a factor concentrating orders in China.

China’s policy stance of protecting domestic supply chains also played a role. China is supporting ship finance to encourage domestic carriers and automakers to place orders with Chinese shipyards. Eom Kyung-a, an analyst at Shinyoung Securities, said, “For the purpose of using ship finance, many Chinese carriers place orders with domestic shipyards.”

Carriers that had ordered PCTCs only from Korean shipbuilders have recently chosen China. Under China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), China Shipbuilding Trading Company signed a contract to build ten 8,200 CEU-class PCTCs with Israeli shipowner Ray Car Carriers. Ray Car Carriers has placed PCTC orders only in Korea for the past 20 years. In April this year, the company also ordered two PCTCs from HD Hyundai Heavy Industries.
